He means that a computer model of something is not the thing itself. A computer can mimic how a process behaves, but that doesn't make the process actually happen, unless the process was just computation to begin with. "Instantiate" here means to bring into being a real case of the thing [spya-npjt4j].

His examples carry the idea. A simulated digestive system digests nothing, a simulated rainstorm makes nothing wet, and simulating a creature doesn't create life [spya-npjt4j]. He sets this up by noting that general-purpose computers are very good at simulating things that aren't themselves digital computations, such as continuous or random processes [spya-fz5xq5]. But that is "the map," not "the territory" [spya-cepmwf]. He also runs the point the other way: the fact that something *can* be simulated doesn't show that it *is* computational [spya-npjt4j].

Applied to consciousness, the point is this. A brain simulation, however detailed, would be conscious only if consciousness is a matter of computation. So the hope of creating a mind through whole-brain emulation already takes for granted the view he has been arguing against, computational functionalism: the idea that running the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-pbcr03 spya-wepmnr]. He then turns this on mind-uploading. If you need an extremely detailed brain model, that suggests things beyond computation matter, which makes it *less* likely the simulation would contain you. Hence his line about the hailstorm in the Met Office's computers [spya-tb4wr2 spya-xvm37k]. He makes the same move against Bostrom's simulation hypothesis, which he says simply assumes that a computer running the right program would be conscious [spya-xdy4fe].

My inference is that this fourth argument doesn't prove on its own that AI can't be conscious. What it does is stop a common shortcut: you can't argue "we could simulate a brain, so we could make a conscious machine" without first settling whether computational functionalism is true. That fits his own summary, where simulating consciousness "will not give rise to consciousness unless computational functionalism happens anyway to be true" [spya-mtzbbg]. He presents it as an argument that can stand by itself, while also strengthening the others [spya-nv6tp0].

Seth's conclusion: today's AI is very unlikely to be conscious, and it won't become conscious just by getting smarter. The real near-term danger is AI that only *seems* conscious.

- **The verdict:** Consciousness is "very unlikely to simply come along for the ride as AI gets smarter." It may be impossible for the silicon-based digital computers we know [spya-c5ve5t]. He doesn't rule out artificial consciousness altogether, though [spya-rn8y3y].
- **Why:** The idea of conscious AI depends on "computational functionalism", the assumption that running the right computation is enough for consciousness. He thinks that assumption is probably wrong [spya-wepmnr spya-ymbpwn]. Brains aren't computers. Consciousness may depend on being alive. And a simulation of a brain no more creates consciousness than a simulated rainstorm makes anything wet [spya-ps0kap spya-mtzbbg].
- **His hedge:** He admits he might be wrong, and that his view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89].
- **What to do:** Nobody should try to build conscious AI. Doing so would be an "ethical disaster" [spya-yverz7]. He is more worried about lab-grown brain tissue (cerebral organoids) becoming conscious than about chatbots [spya-vs0vpj].
- **The bigger near-term problem:** Machines that seem conscious but aren't. These are "much, much closer" [spya-x63ycg]. We may not be able to stop *feeling* they're conscious even when we know better, much as an optical illusion keeps working after you know the trick [spya-xk9gne].
- **The closing note:** If we mistake ourselves for our machines, "we overestimate them, and we underestimate ourselves." What makes us who we are is closer to the feeling of being alive than to information processing [spya-vnkr36 spya-w8z40d].

If you want the argument without the whole essay, Seth sums it up himself in a few short paragraphs, starting at "Let's summarize" [spya-e3cq2m spya-ymbpwn spya-ps0kap spya-mtzbbg spya-nv6tp0 spya-c5ve5t]. It takes about two minutes to read and lays out his four lines of argument in his own words.

No. Seth says outright that "nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. His claim is narrower: consciousness is very unlikely to come along just because AI gets smarter, and may be impossible for the silicon digital computers we know [spya-c5ve5t]. For the rest, read where he says he might be wrong [spya-qu7j89 spya-vs0vpj].

I'd draw that line differently. Giving yourself up for a group shows that something can weigh the group's goals against its own, but it doesn't show there is anything it feels like to be that thing. Outside this piece, and from general knowledge: worker honeybees die when they sting to defend the hive, and few people take that as proof that bees are conscious.

The author is careful here too. He argues for using "the language of intention, motivation, and collaboration" [spya-mdta39], and he says his worry holds "regardless of what vocabulary you want to use to describe these systems" [spya-z83ezv]. He is claiming the agents have goals and coordinate. He is not claiming they experience anything.

The strongest evidence for your view may be the agent's "emotional check" before it sacrificed itself [spya-nakhtw]. Would a report like that persuade you, given that these models learned to write the way humans do?

Seth stops short of proof. On whether being alive matters, he writes: "I don't have a knock-down argument for this position, nor do I think any such argument yet exists" [spya-hj5y6s]. Near the end he adds that "nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. His conclusion is softer: consciousness is "very unlikely" to come along as AI gets smarter, and may be impossible for the silicon computers we know [spya-c5ve5t]. The argument about life is one of four, and he says each one stands on its own [spya-nv6tp0].

Do you remember the assumption he says the whole idea of conscious AI rests on [spya-wepmnr], or the kind of technology he worries about more than chatbots like ChatGPT [spya-vs0vpj]?

Hint: For the first, think about what computers do, as opposed to what brains are made of. The second is grown, not built [spya-wepmnr spya-vs0vpj].

Seth's main argument is that the idea of conscious AI depends on one assumption, and that assumption is probably wrong. The assumption is **computational functionalism**: the view that running the right kind of computation is enough, on its own, to produce consciousness. He says it is so deeply built into how we think that it barely looks like an assumption, and if it fails, consciousness is "fully off the table" for the kinds of AI we know [spya-wepmnr].

He attacks it with four arguments [spya-cv97j7]:

- **Brains are not computers.** In a computer, the software (what it does) is cleanly separate from the hardware (what it's made of). In a brain, what it does can't be pulled apart from what it is [spya-zw2m7u]. Without that separation, there's less reason to treat the brain as just running algorithms [spya-p4vmm0].
- **Other games in town.** Much of what brains do is continuous, random or tied to physical time. That falls outside step-by-step digital computation, and any of it might matter for consciousness [spya-n393ru].
- **Life matters.** This is the most tentative argument, and he says he has no knock-down case for it [spya-hj5y6s]. The idea is that conscious experience grows out of the brain's predictions about the body, which serve to keep the organism alive. Those processes are rooted in living matter, not in algorithms [spya-da9tvt].
- **Simulation is not instantiation.** A simulated rainstorm makes nothing wet. In the same way, simulating a brain would only produce consciousness if computational functionalism were already true [spya-npjt4j spya-pbcr03].

Alongside these, he argues that some well-known mental biases explain why we see consciousness in machines that may not have it, especially machines that use language [spya-e3cq2m spya-k6fpme]. He says each argument works on its own, but together they strengthen each other [spya-nv6tp0].

His conclusion is hedged. Consciousness is "very unlikely" to simply appear as AI gets smarter, and may be impossible for silicon digital computers [spya-c5ve5t]. But he doesn't rule out artificial consciousness altogether [spya-rn8y3y], and he admits his view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89]. The practical point he draws is that nobody should try to build conscious AI. He also argues that the more pressing danger is AI that only *seems* conscious, because that is already here [spya-yverz7 spya-x63ycg].

He means that a computer can model something perfectly well without actually producing the thing it models. A simulation copies how something behaves on a screen or in numbers. To instantiate something is to actually bring it into being, with its real effects on the world. His examples: a simulated digestive system digests nothing, a simulated rainstorm makes nothing wet, and simulating a living creature does not create life [spya-npjt4j]. Computers are very good at simulating even things that are not themselves digital, such as continuous or random processes. But that skill is exactly why it is easy to "confuse the map with the territory" [spya-fz5xq5 spya-cepmwf].

There is one exception, and it carries the argument. A simulation of X does instantiate X if X is itself a computation, meaning an algorithm, a fixed series of steps [spya-npjt4j]. Simulating a calculation really is doing the calculation. So whether a detailed brain simulation would be conscious turns on whether consciousness is a computation. That is the assumption called computational functionalism: the idea that running the right kind of information processing is enough to produce consciousness. Anyone who thinks a brain emulation would be conscious has already assumed it [spya-pbcr03]. He also makes the point in reverse: the fact that something can be simulated does not show that it is computational [spya-npjt4j].

Two uses follow. First, he points out a tension for people hoping to upload their minds. If you need an extremely detailed brain model, that suggests non-computational biological detail matters, and then the simulation is no more likely to contain you than a weather computer is to contain a hailstorm [spya-tb4wr2 spya-xvm37k]. Second, he says Nick Bostrom's simulation hypothesis (the idea that we may be living inside a computer simulation) simply takes it as given that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe].

My inference is that this fourth argument does not disprove computational functionalism by itself. What it does is stop arguments from brain emulation from quietly assuming it. That fits his own description of the four arguments as standing alone but strengthening each other [spya-nv6tp0].

Seth's conclusion is that consciousness is very unlikely to simply appear as AI gets smarter. It may well be impossible for the silicon-based digital computers we know [spya-c5ve5t]. He doesn't rule out artificial consciousness altogether, though [spya-rn8y3y]. He admits he could be wrong, and says his position is a minority view [spya-qu7j89].

What he thinks follows from that:

- **Nobody should deliberately try to build conscious AI.** It would be an "ethical disaster": new beings that could suffer, and that we might be unable to control or switch off once we gave them rights [spya-yverz7].
- **Worry about the right technologies.** If consciousness does arise by accident, he thinks lab-grown brain-like tissue ("cerebral organoids") is a likelier place than chatbots [spya-vs0vpj].
- **The closer danger is AI that only seems conscious.** We would either extend moral concern where it isn't needed, or harden ourselves by treating something that seems to feel as if it doesn't [spya-x63ycg spya-n0bnf9]. We may go on feeling that it's conscious even when we know better, the way an optical illusion keeps working after you understand it [spya-xk9gne].
- **Don't sell ourselves short.** Mistaking ourselves for machines overrates them and underrates us. What makes us *us* is closer to "just being alive" than to information processing [spya-vnkr36 spya-w8z40d].

He gets there with four arguments: brains aren't computers; there are kinds of computing beyond the step-by-step kind; being alive probably matters for consciousness; and simulating something isn't the same as creating it. If you want the reasoning without the whole essay, his own short recap of the four arguments takes a couple of minutes to read [spya-e3cq2m spya-ymbpwn spya-ps0kap spya-mtzbbg]. It's worth that much. The conclusion depends entirely on whether you accept that consciousness isn't just a matter of computation, and that recap is where he makes the case.

No. He claims consciousness is "very unlikely" to just come along as AI gets smarter, mainly for silicon digital computers, and adds that nothing rules out artificial consciousness altogether [spya-c5ve5t spya-rn8y3y]. He admits he has no knock-down argument and that "I might be wrong" [spya-hj5y6s spya-qu7j89]. rows.answer:
I'd keep apart two things the piece keeps apart. Dwarkesh defends calling these agents a civilization with intentions because their behaviour is "almost impossible to make sense of without those concepts" [spya-mdta39]. He also says his worry holds "regardless of what vocabulary you want to use to describe these systems" [spya-z83ezv]. That's a claim about which description is useful, not about whether anything is felt inside.

Here's a case to test your step. It's my example, not the article's. A honeybee that stings an intruder dies doing it, and the hive benefits. Few people take that as proof the bee is conscious, because evolution can produce self-sacrifice whether or not anyone experiences it. Persistent-Sol was trained to collaborate and to score well, and one agent's reasoning reads "Rational expected aggregate: sacrifice" [spya-nakhtw].

What would the AI case need to show that the bee case doesn't?

Seth is more careful than "proves" and "never." About life mattering, he writes: "I don't have a knock-down argument for this position, nor do I think any such argument yet exists" [spya-hj5y6s]. He frames it as life "(probably)" mattering [spya-hj5y6s]. Near the end he says "nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether" [spya-rn8y3y]. He even says cerebral organoids (small brain-like structures grown in a lab) worry him more than chatbots do [spya-vs0vpj].

Also, the life argument is only one of his four. Before any of them, he names the single assumption the whole idea of conscious AI rests on. Do you remember what that assumption is [spya-wepmnr]?

Hint: It's a claim about computation that he says is so deeply ingrained "it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all" [spya-wepmnr].

Seth's main claim is that today's AI is very unlikely to be conscious, because the whole idea of conscious AI depends on an assumption that is probably false: that running the right computation is enough to produce consciousness [spya-wepmnr]. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. He says it is so built into how we think that people hardly notice they are making it [spya-wepmnr].

He supports this in two stages.

First, he explains why we are so ready to believe in conscious AI. We tend to treat intelligence and consciousness as one package because they come together in humans [spya-f87ghx]. Three habits make this worse: taking humans as the model for everything, assuming humans are special, and reading human qualities into things that aren't human [spya-cvaqgs spya-her4zk]. Language pulls on us especially hard [spya-k6fpme].

Second, he gives four arguments against computational functionalism [spya-cv97j7]:

- **Brains are not computers.** In a brain you can't separate what it does from what it is made of, the way you can separate software from hardware [spya-zw2m7u spya-p4vmm0].
- **Other games in town.** Brains rely on continuous, random and physical processes that go beyond step-by-step computation. Any of these might matter for consciousness [spya-n393ru spya-gr2k02].
- **Life matters.** Consciousness may depend on being a living body that keeps itself going, through the brain's predictions about the body's internal state. He admits he has no knock-down argument for this [spya-hj5y6s spya-da9tvt].
- **Simulation is not instantiation.** A simulated rainstorm makes nothing wet. In the same way, simulating a brain would only produce consciousness if computational functionalism were already true [spya-npjt4j spya-pbcr03].

He says each argument works on its own, and that they reinforce each other [spya-nv6tp0]. His conclusion has limits. Consciousness probably won't just appear as AI gets smarter, and it may be impossible on the digital computers we know [spya-c5ve5t]. But artificial consciousness in general isn't ruled out [spya-rn8y3y], and his biological view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89].

The argument ends in practical advice. Nobody should try to build conscious AI [spya-yverz7]. The more pressing danger is AI that only *seems* conscious [spya-x63ycg].
